Hi Samira — Ben from Solutions Engineering. Added a short test kit and lab script examples you can run (no binary attachments, just steps). Highlights below:

1) Test methodology (quick):
- Warm baseline: run steady QPS for 30m to populate prefix cache and KV cache.
- Inject burst: increase synthetic traffic to target multiplier (e.g., 15x) for 90s across same request distribution.
- Observe: p95/p99/p999 across tokens, queue depth, GPU utilization, and fallback triggers.

2) What you'll see (typical):
- First 10-15s: small latency bump; continuous batching increases samples/threading to amortize kernel launch.
- 15-90s: if cache hit rate drops, system will proactively switch to a compatible quantized variant and increase KV-cache reservation for hot prefixes. Expect p99 to be within 2-3x baseline for conversational loads, p999 may spike but will be bounded by fallback thresholds.

3) Acceptance matrix (summary):
- Action thresholds: 20% tail-latency increase -> trigger batching floor increase; 50% -> quantized fallback; 200% sustained -> regional fanout.

Drive link with the perf runbook and lab scripts: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a2b3c-burst-recovery

Happy to run a short remote lab with your engineers.

– Ben Carter
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: RFP Q: behavior under burst saturation / recovery expectations

Samira — technical detail from the runtime side. Quoting Ben below for context.

- KV cache & prefix retention: we maintain per-prefix hotset tables; during bursts we allocate up to a tunable emergency pool (configurable per-customer) before eviction policies kick in. For RLHF-style long-context workloads this preserves hot prefix hits for the first 20-40s of a burst.
- Batching strategy: continuous batching with adaptive latency caps (we enforce per-request max wait of 15ms for interactive SKUs; during sustained bursts that cap may be temporarily relaxed as a controlled parameter).
- Quantized fallback: we support int8/int4 compatible model variants with identical tokenizer/IO contracts. Fallback occurs with staged ramp (10% traffic -> 50% -> 100%) to allow A/B signal checks.
- Regional fanout: transparent routing duplicates the request to a secondary region only if local health and headroom metrics both exceed configured thresholds; duplicate responses are deduplicated at the control plane.

Empirical numbers from a recent internal replay (interleaved conv-turns workload): baseline p99=120ms, during synthetic 15x burst p99 peaked at 390ms after first fallbacks, and returned to within 130% of baseline within 75s once prefix cache warmed back. We'll include the raw replay artifact in the runbook.

Karthik Iyer
Principal Inferencing Engineer, Redwood Inference
